title: Price alerts
context: Lets users set price alerts ("tell me when AAPL reaches 250"). AlertService is a singleton; each alert listens to the live price feed, which ticks many times per second. Users can delete alerts in the app, and alerts expire after a set time.

points.title: Feed listeners are never removed
points.why: delete() and expiry only remove the alert from the map. The listener stays registered with the feed and keeps a reference to the alert, so memory grows with every alert ever created and deleted alerts keep firing.
points.fix: Keep the subscription handle returned by subscribe and unsubscribe it in delete() and on expiry.

points.title: Alert fires on every tick
points.why: Once the price is above the target, every price update sends another notification, so the user gets spammed many times per second.
points.fix: Fire once: remove the alert atomically before notifying (for example only notify if alerts.remove(id) returned it) and unsubscribe.

points.title: Scheduled task dies on the first exception
points.why: If expireOldAlerts throws once (for example the notifier is down), scheduleAtFixedRate silently cancels every future run, so alerts never expire again and nobody is told.
points.fix: Catch and log exceptions inside the task, or use Spring's @Scheduled, which keeps running and logs errors.

points.title: Unbounded queue in the notification pool
points.why: newFixedThreadPool uses an unbounded queue. During a market spike, or when the notifier is slow, tasks pile up without limit until the JVM runs out of memory.
points.fix: Use a ThreadPoolExecutor with a bounded queue and a rejection policy, or hand notifications to a message queue.

points.title: Executors outside Spring's lifecycle
points.why: These thread pools are never shut down, so threads leak on context restarts (tests, hot reload) and in-flight notifications are cut off on shutdown.
points.fix: Use Spring-managed TaskScheduler and ThreadPoolTaskExecutor beans, or shut the pools down in @PreDestroy.
